t: LeetCode 195 — Tenth Line: Three Ways to Print Exactly One Line
o:
You are handed `file.txt` and must print **only its 10th line** — no other output, and nothing at all if the file has fewer than ten lines.

**Example:** with a file containing `Line 1` through `Line 10`, the script must print exactly `Line 10`. If the file stopped at `Line 9`, the correct behavior is to print an empty result.

There are no algorithmic constraints here — the problem is really about composing Unix text tools and handling the edge cases: short files, very large files (so avoid slurping everything into memory unless you must), and line numbering that starts at 1. As the note suggests, at least three clean one-liners exist: a `head`/`tail` pipeline, an `awk` line-counter filter, and a `sed` address.
k: `awk 'NR == 10 { print; exit }' file.txt` streams the file with a constant-memory line counter and stops reading after the target line — the most idiomatic scalable answer.
`sed -n '10p'` suppresses sed's default echo (`-n`) and prints only where the line-number address matches; on shorter files it silently outputs nothing.
`head -n 10 file.txt | tail -n 1` composes two simple tools: take the first ten lines, keep the last of those.
If the file has fewer than 10 lines, all three approaches correctly produce no output.

a.i: `head -n 10 file.txt | tail -n 1` reads just the first ten lines and passes them to `tail`, which keeps the last one. It is the easiest solution to reason about: bounded work (ten lines), and if the file ends early, the pipeline simply has nothing left to print.
s: Pipe file.txt through `head -n 10` to keep only the first ten lines.
Pipe that into `tail -n 1` to emit the last of them (the 10th line).
If the file was shorter, the stream is empty and nothing is printed.

c.python:
# Shell problem — reference Python equivalent of: head -n 10 file.txt | tail -n 1
with open('file.txt') as f:
    first_ten = [line for _, line in zip(range(10), f)]
if first_ten:
    print(first_ten[-1], end='')

a.t: O(1) beyond the first ten lines — only ten lines are ever read.
a.sp: O(1) — at most ten lines are held.

a.i: awk automatically numbers every input record in the variable `NR`, so `awk 'NR == 10 { print; exit }' file.txt` prints the tenth line and quits immediately — it never reads past the target line of a huge file. This is the recommended one-liner.
s: Use the pattern `NR == 10` so the action fires only on the tenth record.
Print `$0` (the whole line) and call `exit` to stop reading further input.
a.t: O(L) — reads only up to the tenth line (L characters of it), then exits.
a.sp: O(1) — one line buffer, regardless of file size.

a.i: `sed -n '10p' file.txt` treats the line number as an address: with `-n` disabling automatic printing, the `p` command echoes only lines matching the address. It reads the entire file (no early exit), but expresses the intent in a single terse command.
s: Pass `-n` so lines are not printed by default.
Attach the `p` command to the address `10` so only the tenth line is printed.

c.python:
# Reference equivalent of: sed -n '10p' file.txt
lines = open('file.txt').read().splitlines()
if len(lines) >= 10:
    print(lines[9])

a.t: O(F) — sed scans the whole file (F total characters) since it has no exit-on-match.
a.sp: O(1) for sed itself; the indexed-language variants shown load or stream accordingly.

w:
**Which to use:** in an interview say `awk 'NR == 10 { print; exit }'` first — it is one pass, constant memory, and stops early on huge files. Mention `sed -n '10p'` as the shortest form and the `head | tail` pipeline as the tool-composition alternative.

**Pitfalls and edge cases:**
- Fewer than ten lines: every approach must print nothing (no blank line noise, no error).
- Very large files: avoid reading the whole file into memory; `head -n 10` and `awk ... exit` both cap the work.
- Trailing newline / CRLF endings can shift what "the 10th line" looks like byte-wise; strip `\r` if the file came from Windows.

**Follow-ups:** print the last line (`tail -n 1`), a range of lines (`sed -n '5,8p'` or `awk 'NR>=5 && NR<=8'`), every 10th line, or the nth column of a file.
